At this point, I would like to rule out his public appearances or his appearances in any other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Obviously you can only testify about what you saw or heard. Sir, did the Crisis Staff order that Stari Grad be levelled to the ground after the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff didn't issue such an order. I don't know who would it be that the Crisis Staff could issue order to? The Crisis Staff did not have any instruments, any tools, to issue such an order and have it implemented. I don't know. I'm sure that such an order could not have been implemented. In any case, the Crisis Staff could not have ensured the implementation of any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what contacts did you have in your official capacity with the Ljubija mine company?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my official capacity, my contacts with the Ljubija mine were with the CEO of the company. We were talking about the recruits who were to be mobilised from his company. Actually, to be more precise, they were comprised by the additional mobilisation. We discussed the matter in terms of the mine giving conscripts for the army but still being able to maintain the level of their production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- I'm not sure what the correct word would be. But did you make sure that equipment from the Ljubija mine company was put at the disposal of the army or of the Crisis Staff? Was that part of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not concern myself with the equipment of the mine. You said something else, but I can't remember what you asked me. When there was a request of the army for a piece of machinery or a vehicle to be mobilised for the army, I would forward that request to the company director, and they were then under the obligation to put such a vehicle or machinery at the disposal of the army. If the company could not do without such a piece of machinery or equipment, then we would set up priorities together. In any case, it was the army's priorities that came first rather than the company's priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you then, if I understand you correctly, you would convey the army's request to Mr. Marjanovic for specific equipment that the army needed. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We forwarded such requests to all the companies, including the mine, and we additionally mobilised materiel and technical equipment from those companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One question before the break: Was Mr. Marjanovic a member or did he attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic was not a member of the Crisis Staff, and I don't remember him ever having attended the Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I can slip in one more question to finish the subject, was the equipment of the Ljubija mine company used to bulldoze and flatten Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not under the authority of the body that I headed, and I don't have any information on that. I didn't participate in that, so I cannot give you any clarification on that. It was not done on my order, if this was done. And under whose orders, you should ask somebody else. I'm sure they would be able to give you a better answer than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To stay in the context, and not to come back to this question again, on today's transcript, page 48, line 7, you said: "Everybody in the presidency, including Dr. Stakic, asked for these illegal acts on the territory of Prijedor to be put an end to." Question: "Specifically, what illegal acts are you referring to?" Your answer was: "We are talking about plunder, killings, disorder, arson, and other similar things." Later on, you added that you never discussed -- or it was never discussed at least in your presence in the framework of the Crisis Staff the establishment of camps or reception centres or collection centres, whatever term you want to use. Isn't the conclusion correct that following this, when you're discussing reactions on plunder and killings and disorder, these camps were not designed as a reaction on plunder, killings, and disorder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question can be answered by those who set up these camps or investigation centres. I've told you that I didn't take any action, measure, or procedure relative to these collection centres under my authority. Secondly, that these centres were never discussed at the Crisis Staff meetings. Why and for what reason, I don't know. And who was it who should have put that question on the agenda, I don't know. I did what I was supposed to do, and the only matters that I was supposed to put on the agenda when this was needed were the matters that fell under my jurisdictions and that were within my purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But once again, you stated that "everybody in the presidency, including Dr. Stakic, tried to react and to prevent these plunder, killings, disorder..." And would it therefore be correct that in this context, to put an end to these illegal acts, to quote your own words, these killings, disorder, the establishment of camps in this context was never discussed as an appropriate measure or response to these killings and plunder? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct. We never discussed that. Why and who retained this information, at what level, within which circle, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then finally, we have to decide on the document tendered by the Prosecution. The conclusions of the 6th of August, 1995 of the Republika Srpska Prijedor Municipality War Presidency. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We think that it's outside of the scope of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have already previously the comment -- our comments after the deliberations of the Chamber. Therefore, admitted into evidence as S403A and B respectively. The trial stays adjourned until half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Koumjian, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, from your office in the same building as the SUP building, did you hear screams and other sounds, or did you see things that made you aware of prisoners being abused in that building and in the parking lot to that building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my position, the position that I worked in and from that room, I could see people being brought in to the SUP building. And every time, a different door was used. The next door was used. And I could see people being brought in through the parking lot, and they were taken to the restaurant. And this is where two offices were that served for those people who were taken in. During my working hours, while I was there, I didn't see any abuse going on. I didn't see anybody being beaten up among those people who had been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear any screams?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not during my working hours. I didn't hear any screams. In the afternoon I was never there. I was either at home or in the early warning and reporting centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did you live at that time? What area or village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Miljakovci which is 5 and a half kilometres south of the town which is on the right bank of the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So would that be correct that that would be towards the Brdo region?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the Sana River in relation to Brdo, a bit higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In your travels around the municipality, did you see homes destroyed, either by shells or by arson, in the area of the Hambarine and the wider area of Brdo, and in the Kozarac, Kamicani, Kozarusa area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that houses had been burnt down and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you visit the area around Brisevo near Ljubija and see similar destruction?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't go in that direction. I went through Kozarac towards Banja Luka, and that was on the way home I could see Carakovo and parts of Hambarine on the left bank of the Sana River. I could see that these parts were destroyed. But I've already said that there was no need for me to go towards Ljubija during the war operations. My job simply didn't take me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your examination three names of employees of non-Serbian ethnicity, I believe all Muslims, who worked with you after you became the secretary. Dzevad Habibovic, Kerim Mesanovic, and Muhamed Burazerovic. Were you aware that all three of them were taken to the Omarska camp in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and answer because the nodding is not reflected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not nodding. I'm going to answer the question that was put to me. Now, you have confused me. Can you please repeat the question. In the meantime, I have forgotten the question. And if you could repeat these names, I will answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Certainly. I named three Muslims who I believe -- I understood from your direct examination or from your earlier examination worked for you when you were the secretary of the secretariat of national defence for the municipality. And forgive my pronunciation, I believe they were Dzevad Habibovic, Kerim Mesanovic, and Muhamed Burazerovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me a correction, they didn't work for me. They worked in the body that I headed. As far as these three individuals are concerned, subsequently I learned that they had been taken in by the Ministry of the Interior, but I don't have any information of their further movements and eventually of their lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you learn that Muhamed Burazerovic was killed in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently I learned that Burazerovic was a victim of the war operations, but I don't know exactly how and where it happened. I'm not aware of the circumstances of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that every citizen has a duty to report abuses and crimes and that a body such as the Crisis Staff would have a duty to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. direct the attention of competent bodies to any abuse by the police or the army. Did you, as a member of the Crisis Staff and National Defence Council, ever initiate any discussion about the crimes that you were aware of against the civilian population of non-Serbian ethnicity in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we establish a link between your last question and your question before last, I can only say something that I have already said in my testimony. When the first person out of the three that you've mentioned failed to turn up for work, and when I learned that he had been brought in by the police, I went to the chief of the police and asked for the explanation as to how this happened and under what circumstances. What I received as the answer was very ugly. I was told that I was protecting some people, that I gave them shelter in my body, and then the receiver was slammed down on me. After that, I never asked for any explanations. I never initiated any discussions because all of these things were under the jurisdiction of this man who reacted so badly to my first telephone intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in the National Defence Council or the Crisis Staff, prior to the 22nd of May, prior to the incident at Hambarine, were there discussions about preparing for conflict with the Muslim and Croat populations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the session that I attended. There was no discussion about preparations of conflicts between ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your testimony that you were aware that an artillery unit was moved from the front in Croatia back to Prijedor in May, in early May. And as soon as I can find the document, I will have it shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown S61 -- excuse me, that's not it. S345, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While that's being prepared, sir, did the police enforce a curfew in Prijedor after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't remember when the curfew was introduced. There was a curfew in force for a certain period of time, but I don't know exactly when that was. And I do know that it was the Ministry of the Interior that introduced this curfew. But that was something that they had the right to do. It was within their legal authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, the Ministry of the Interior or police did not introduce -- they enforced the curfew. Is that correct? They were the ones that would arrest people that would violate the curfew. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The enforcement of the curfew was under the authority of the police; however, I don't know whether anybody was arrested, where, or when. I simply can't provide you with any facts on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in a moment. First, regarding the movement of the artillery, if you look at S345 which you should have in front of you now, in point number 2 of this combat report dated the 3rd of May 1992 and marked "strictly confidential," the second sentence under point number 2 indicates that "in the course of the 2nd and 3rd of May, one 105-millimetre Howitzer battery and one anti-armour artillery battery of the 343rd Motorised Brigade were relocated to the Prijedor area in order to strengthen the units and the wider Prijedor/Ljubija/Kozarac area. The units have taken up their positions." Do these dates, sir, in this order - realising that it's a military order that you may or may not have seen marked "strictly confidential" - do these dates correspond to your recollection of when that artillery was moved?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I have a general knowledge of the relocation of those units, but under whose orders and when that happened I can't tell you because I never had precise information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, but could the witness be shown again S28.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, S28 was the minutes of the 5th of May of the National Defence Council. Isn't it correct, sir, that that was the session and that was the body that introduced the curfew that was enforced by the police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This body was not authorised, nor did it have ability to introduce a curfew. It could have proposed that if discussion was taking place on disorders and law and order. They could have proposed that, and they could have forwarded that proposal to the Ministry of the Interior. And the Ministry of the Interior was the only body that could have introduced a curfew having taken into account the situation in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the curfew, according to this decision, was introduced by the National Defence Council. I'm not asking you what its legal authority was. Isn't it correct that at that session, the curfew was introduced and that this document was signed by Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing the wording of this document, but what I'm saying is that the discussion did not take this form, and I'm also saying that the Crisis Staff could not have introduced a curfew because the law on the Ministry of the Interior regulated precisely who it was who was able to introduce a curfew. And no further or subsequent document derogated that law. So the only person who could have introduced a curfew was the minister of the interior, maybe upon the proposal of the Crisis Staff. But it was only the minister of the interior who had legal authority to introduce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about mobilisations for a moment. The Crisis Staff or National Defence Council, did they order you, direct you in any way to mobilise individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't order, direct me, or do anything similar. Even if they had, I could not have acted on any such instructions because in my work, I was governed by the law on national defence. I've already said in my testimony that it is the president of the republic who orders mobilisation, gives the order to the minister of the defence, and then it goes down the line of command. Since we had problems that I've already mentioned, mobilisation was carried out, but the units were not mobilised to the full strength. Then conscripts were appealed to by public notices to report to their respective units. Mobilisation could have been carried out by a general, public notice. Those were posters that were -- that were to be seen all around the town, and then people would report to their units, having read those notifications. So this was maybe what the Crisis Staff could do and they did. But it was not in the purview -- within the purview of the Crisis Staff to order mobilisation of any of the structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S61.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, while that's being prepared, during 1992 and throughout the war until Dayton, would it be correct to say that people at least of Serbian ethnicity saw that responding to the mobilisation was a patriotic duty?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very general political question. And it will largely depend on every individual, every conscript. We did not carry out a public poll, and this can be accepted as a general position. But I can't give you a precise view of what people may have thought. What I can tell you is that in keeping with the law, everybody was duty-bound to report to mobilisation and report to their units, or when posters were distributed all over the town, then they had to respond to that call according to their military specialisation that was recorded in their service books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me try to be more specific. Leaders of the SDS party, would it be correct that they made public pronouncements that responding to the mobilisation was a patriotic duty, and that it was their position that it would have been wrong under their stated political position for people to use family connections, for example, to attempt to evade mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the first part of your question, I can accept it. And my answer would be that yes, there had been appeals invoking patriotic duty to that effect. And I cannot answer the second part of your question because I don't accept the premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps I wasn't clear. What you do not accept, if I understand you, is that you're saying leaders of the SDS did not try to get their family members excused from military service just as a favour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown the exhibit on which this matter is discussed, or it's presumed. So I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not discussing an exhibit. I'm asking the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then it is not in evidence. It's presumed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to argue the point in front of the witness, but if counsel has put in evidence that they have offered their 92 bis on this point. These are the questions I'm directing my questions to. It's not that I'm saying this happened. I'm talking about why it would not happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you'll allow me, may I answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please wait for the Judge to rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objection dismissed after deliberation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you may answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colleague asked if certain members of the SDS tried in some way to protect themselves or their family members. On that issue, I said in one statement that I gave that I, as chief of section, had encountered a similar situation; namely, deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor adopted a conclusion at one of their sessions to the effect that they, as deputies of the Municipal Assembly, should not be called up into the army. And they justified it by saying that they, as deputies, are very busy with their municipal duties. However, since I always followed the law on the army, which was a higher legal enactment, I could not accept that conclusion adopted by the deputies of the Municipal Assembly. Therefore, I conducted mobilisation as envisaged by the law. And because of that, I encountered certain problems because some people insisted that I should respect the conclusion I spoke about, rather than follow the law, if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, that wasn't my question. And I appreciate you trying to answer my question, Mr. Budimir. If you can try to keep your answers confined to the question, perhaps we can move a little faster. I'm sorry, I'm going a little slowly today. Sir, to be direct, did Dr. Stakic ever contact you and ask you not to mobilise someone? Yes or no, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody asked some favours at one time or another, not only Stakic but everybody. But I never acted on such requests. I did what I was asked to -- what I was required to do by law. I also had major conflicts with deputies on that score, but I don't want to waste any more of our time elaborating on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever mobilise Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After he left his office of president of the municipality, Dr. Stakic reported to the command of the 43rd Brigade to his colleague, Zeljko Macura, and spent some time in the army. I don't know exactly how much time. Probably until he returned to political life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, S61 is the document which is before you now. It's dated the 22nd of May. First, if I could ask you, on the 22nd of May, this is a date which we all believe in this courtroom was the date of the incident at the Hambarine checkpoint. Do you recall the incident in question? I'm not asking if you were there, but do you recall that day of the incident at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the story about this incident, but I cannot recollect the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff or the National Defence Council or any body of which you were a member meet on that day to discuss a response to that incident?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I can remember. I don't remember myself attending such a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you briefly explain, if you know, which units the following numerical designations refer to. War unit 4777?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember these numbers exactly. I think those were units which had points of mobilisation assembly in Banja Luka. It may have been an armoured brigade, but I cannot remember their code numbers, apart from this 8316, which was the 5th Kozara Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was 3507 a Banja Luka rocket unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out that possibility, but I can't say for sure. I can't remember all the codes. You are asking too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about TO 8316, does that-- are you able to recollect what that was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said, it's the 5th Kozara Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sir, do you recall seeing this order -- excuse me, decision on mobilisation on the territory of Prijedor dated the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is not very clear, but in view of the job I was doing, I don't rule out the possibility that I had had access to this document. But it was not drafted in my agency. It was drafted by one of the technical services. I can't rule it out one way or another. Whenever an issue fell within my competence, I always tried to gain access to all the necessary information and see what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned posters that would appear in town instructing individuals to report to their war units. Were these posters signed in the name of the Crisis Staff, the name of the National Defence Council? How were they signed, if at all? Did you sign them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these posters, I mentioned them only as one of the possibilities used. Whenever general mobilisation was announced, one of the possibilities was to announce it by posters, on the media, and every other way. We tried to use every possibility to get military conscripts to report as soon as possible to their points of report. However, at that particular time we didn't have access to printworks, and we couldn't make these posters. As for announcement of mobilisation through the media, it said "the command of such and such a corps is urging military conscripts to report to this and that unit," et cetera. There were also appeals by all political and social forces to get the men to report -- to respond to military callups, but it was usually the military units themselves that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appealed to the conscripts to report wherever they were supposed to report. That was the official demand, callup, made by military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you did not have access to printworks at this time. Isn't it true that on the 30th of April, after the takeover, placards appeared throughout Prijedor explaining the reasons for the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that we didn't have access to the printworks. I said we didn't use that possibility, which was envisaged by the legislation for announcing various things. As for posters, everybody had access to that. There were all sorts of posters with various announcements. I said that we didn't use that way because we mostly made announcements through the media, public appeals, and especially in this case, callups were served through the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did posters appear after the takeover signed on behalf of the Crisis Staff explaining the takeover?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, sorry, no, we were talking about mobilisation all this time, and now you come up with government and takeover. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the takeover on the 30th of April, did posters appear in town explaining the takeover and saying why the Crisis Staff had taken power?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any posters about the Crisis Staff taking over because the Crisis Staff never took over power. All I know is that after the takeover, there was an information programme where representatives of the government stated the reasons. And I don't remember any posters written by the Crisis Staff saying that they took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, before the army attacked Hambarine and Kozarac, did you discuss those issues, the security situation, and what the army response would be in any of the bodies that you were a member of, Crisis Staff or National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Many issues were discussed, but precisely in the sense that you are referring to, possible responses and details, I don't remember anything of the sort. I don't remember there was any talk about possible outcomes and premises and how one should respond to them. I don't remember anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, surely you would remember, wouldn't you, if you discussed attacking an area of Prijedor, of the army attack an area? Wouldn't that be something that would stick in your memory, even now, 11 years later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no discussions about anyone attacking anyone else, especially not the army. And I personally had no information at all about any attacks, and I already said I had no information at all about takeovers or attacks of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, on Tuesday, you were talking about the Crisis Staff and the agenda. On page 21, beginning on line 12, you said: "Even when we were formulating the agenda, I believe there wasn't a precise agenda. There was a broad item, political security situation. And within that item, all the different questions were discussed." Sir, would the army attacking, shelling, an area of Prijedor, in your opinion, fall within this broad item of political security situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not arguing with what you say about the army attacking. I am not arguing about whether it needed to be discussed or not. But at the sessions which I attended, there was no discussion about this shelling and about this event. I'm not disputing what you say but this organ, this body, did not discuss that because as I said earlier, the army never informed us of any of its activities or measures that it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what is the most memorable discussion that you can recall now of the Crisis Staff? What issue of importance do you remember now that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the most important issue we discussed was when we wanted to stop the unrest in town and when we asked the army and the police to restore order, and we even suggested to help them resolve the situation concerning military conscripts. They refused that, and the situation eventually didn't change. Our possibilities were thus exhausted, and we could not make any more demands on them to take measures so as to restore law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the Crisis Staff issued demands upon the people in the Hambarine and Kozarac areas, threatening them just before the army attacked?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that the Crisis Staff never issued anything of the kind. I don't remember anything of the kind, nor did such a document pass through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S383.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't it part of the statute of -- or whatever the legal document is called of the Crisis Staff and of the Municipal Assembly to ensure the security and safety of the citizens of the municipality? Wasn't that one of your basic responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The safety and security of the citizens in the municipality fell within the competence of the Ministry of the Interior. In the normal course of things, the Crisis Staff, as a body which took care of the overall situation in the territory of the assembly and all aspects of social life, discussed this issue and demanded from the Ministry of the Interior to take the necessary measures to restore law and order and all the other things that we have already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The correct document is S389.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, S389 is a page from Kozarski Vjesnik of the 29th of May 1992. And you will see bordered in yellow highlighters several articles with various dates signed "Crisis Staff." One is dated the 23rd of May 1992. The one begins "at 1900 hours on 22nd May..." If you could find that article.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it under number 2. Here, on my paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can look at the third paragraph where it indicates: "The Crisis Staff hereby orders the population of Hambarine local commune and other local communes in the area, that is, all the citizens of Muslim and other ethnicities, to hand over the perpetrators of this crime, particularly Aziz Aliskovic and his group, who are the direct organisers of this clash, to the Prijedor public security station, or the competent military organs by 1200 hours today, Saturday, 23 May." And that's the end of the sentence on the translation I have. The next sentence is: "This crime has exhausted all deadlines and promises, and the Crisis Staff no longer can nor is it willing to guarantee the security of the population of the above-mentioned villages in this area." Sir, isn't it a fact that the Crisis Staff made that demand on Hambarine and, in fact, the army followed up on that threat and attacked the town, shelling it with tank fire?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on these conclusions from the newspaper, I cannot accept this as proof that there were appeals from people in the Crisis Staff to do this. I don't dispute that part, but it was within the competence of the police. It was their job. I don't see why anybody would write this if it was in the competence of the police to take these men into custody. I stand by my viewpoint that as an agenda at the session -- as an agenda item at the session which I attended, this was not discussed in such a way. And as a rule, the Crisis Staff would not be signed. It was the person heading the Crisis Staff, the responsible person in the Crisis Staff, that was normally signed. So I stand by my earlier stated point that it was not discussed in the Crisis Staff; the Crisis Staff could not issue such an order; it could only ask the police and the army to take whatever measures were in their competence to redress the situation and to restore order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff or Dr. Stakic, to your knowledge, ever issue any denial of this article or of other public media statements on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't even remember this article, and I don't remember any denial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, surely you talked in the Crisis Staff about the visit of foreign journalists to the Omarska and Trnopolje camps in August of 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We did not surely talk about this visit. I had no information about that visit, and the Crisis Staff did not discuss visits by journalists in my presence. I only saw it on videotape. I believe it was Mico Kovacevic who gave some sort of interview to journalists. But nobody gave him instructions as to what to say on behalf of the Crisis Staff, nor did he later report to the Crisis Staff as to what was said and what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify something, when the Crisis Staff was first activated, was the Executive Board at that time suspended? In other words, was the Crisis Staff meeting in place of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff assumed the duties and obligations of the organs of the Municipal Assembly, and they were not supposed to meet in that period. When they were not able to meet, rather. I don't know whether that lasted for 10 or 15 days in the last quarter of May, or perhaps the first half of June. I believe the Executive Board did not meet during that period. But as soon as the situation was a little normalised, every member of the Executive Board continued to work in his office and occasional sessions of the Executive Board were held. And sometimes the sessions of the two bodies perhaps intertwined. But it is quite possible that at a certain time, the Executive Board could exist in parallel with the Crisis Staff. A large number of deputies that was required was not able to meet for a while, until August or perhaps end September. I don't think I can place this in time precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene once again, but on page 71, line 6, when asked about a visit by journalists, you answered: "I only saw it on videotape." Could you please tell this Chamber when you saw this on videotape and -- please, first, when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have seen it on TV or maybe journalists from Prijedor showed it to me. I can't remember. I can't give you a precise answer to that question. I remember having seen Mr. Kovacevic. I recognise his mannerism. He was talking to somebody. But when it was that I saw it, when it was that I became aware of that, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But wouldn't it be normal when you would have seen it on TV, to answer this question "I saw it on TV" instead of "I saw it on a videotape." Please try to concentrate on this question. Did you receive a videotape on this? And by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not receive a cassette. I saw this footage on television. I was not in the position to have that videocassette in my hands. And I apologise if you have misunderstood my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Koumjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We had a videotape that we're apparently having some trouble with, S11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be an appropriate time to have a break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, or I could move to another subject -- sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, the trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Koumjian, would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, you told us that the Executive Board may not have been functioning at the time the Crisis Staff or may have functioned at the same time. I'd like now to play a video of chronicles of Prijedor. It's S11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would my learned friend be so kind and quote what the witness said, and the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have it because it's today. He said it just before the break. I don't have it on my monitor. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the video booth, then, please play the video. Just for the record, this is S11. And the transcript, we have it set to be cued to begin at page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, a few questions about that video. First, in the initial, would it be correct to place the time of this interview, given that the announcer talks about combat activity in Ljubija and Colonel Arsic refers to military activity -- renewed fighting he said, in Rizvanovici and Biscani and there's also the announcer talked about the town being quiet after two months and that this programme is likely broadcast in late July, the second half of July of 1992? If you're unsure, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I want to avoid that a question seems to be a misleading one. You should be aware that on the top page, it reads "produced by TV Banja Luka, 30th of June, 1992".

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that refers to the top -- that's above the line refers to the programme on the tape before the one we just saw. There are various programmes on S11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know. But maybe it's then of assistance also to put to the witness the date of the production of TV Banja Luka, of this part of this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll check and see -- I don't have that page, if there is one, that shows the date. Ms. Karper will be looking for it. In the meantime, just in the interests of time, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would the Prosecution be able Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to tell us whether Mr. Stakic gave this interview the same day as Mr. Arsic or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution can't testify in this case. And therefore, this question is more or less a rhetorical one. But I think it is helpful to have the end of this document where the date of the production is reflected. And then we all can draw our own conclusions whether this was on the same day or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There's no production credits at the end of this segment. There are credits, excuse me, but there's no date given. And that's on ERN page 03065777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, at least, for the attempt. So we have to draw the conclusions out of the context and the content of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, Dr. Stakic in his interview indicated, and I'm reading from page 14: "During war operations, there was a Crisis Staff in Prijedor that has now been renamed the war presidency by a decision from the government and the Presidency of the Serbian Republic. But as soon as the initial combat activity subsided, we activated the executive committee, and it now operates normally." Would I be correct, sir, in your opinion, in concluding that the executive committee was suspended at least during the initial phase of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the terminology that you have been using, I don't know enough about it. But I said that at the moment when the Crisis Staff took over the duties of the Municipal Assembly and its organs, for a brief period of time, for objective conditions and events in the territory, the Executive Board did not meet, and that lasted for a short period of time. As soon as the secretaries of various secretariats as members of the Executive Board were able to do their job properly, then the Executive Board started functioning again. So I don't see that there could have been any sort of suspension. I don't know whether we understand each other. I believe that what I am saying is more correct. The Executive Board was never formally, legally suspended; it only stopped being convened for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. In the interview with Colonel Arsic, he begins by indicating "I would first like to make one remark. I am not the only one who is well-informed about the events taking place in Prijedor. All government organs also know very well what is going on in Prijedor." Would you agree with what Colonel Arsic said in that interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since all of us here are trying as much as possible to arrive at the truth, I can try and share my views with you. In this specific case, you can see how a systematic and experienced person answers questions. As soon as he is asking a question, he makes some reservations. If that same question had been put to Dr. Stakic, who was an inexperienced young person, he would have accepted -- he would have taken the bite and continued talking. But this person here has tried to pass on the buck, if I may say so, on to other persons, although he had never reported on the activities of the army to any of these people. The only persons he reported to were his superiors in the army. I don't hold it against him because that is exactly what he was supposed to do under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did Mr. Baltic attend meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Baltic did attend the Crisis Staff meetings. Conditionally speaking, he didn't attend all of them, but yes, he did attend them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall, did Mr. Baltic inform the Crisis Staff through written reports on implementations of conclusions of the municipal Crisis Staff or decisions of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I only know that the decisions were made by the Crisis Staff, and that Mr. Baltic was then submitting them to the Municipal Assembly for ratification. I believe that this session was at the end of July or beginning of August. I can't remember exactly because I did not attend that session at which the decisions were ratified. I believe that once these decisions were ratified, the Crisis Staff stopped being convened, and that there was no further feedback on the ratification of the Crisis Staff decisions at any of the meetings of the Crisis Staff after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, before we leave this area, may I ask the witness to show to the Defence and to the Prosecution the exhibit as admitted under Exhibit S11A where it clearly reads that the videotape from 000 to 0444, pages 12 to 14, is a production of TV Banja Luka, 30th of June 1992. And if I am wrong, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position on that is that this tape 0444 includes several programmes that were put on one videotape. The date that you're referring to, I believe, reflects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: These are the text just immediately beforehand read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, but there's a line -- I believe that that date refers to the programme immediately before what was read out. That's my belief, and from what the context of the interview, it's very clear it's late July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May this document also please be shown to the Defence that both parties have the same possibility to comment on this. It's only the right to be heard on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness might help us in one respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, Vidovdan, is that a holiday that has a specific -- does it fall on the same day each year? Can you help us on that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 28 June every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we may just comment, Your Honour, briefly, if I'm correct in understanding the Court, the exhibit that the Court just tendered as admitted S11A, it is the paragraph that is on the first page of that that seems to be similar to the one that the Prosecution has shown the witness. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One is the rough translation, and the other seems to be a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it might be important, and I think the Court suggested this, and I apologise if I didn't hear it because we were conferring, I think 11A should be shown to the witness because it is in our opinion somewhat different than the rough translations when it involves the questions that are specifically being put to the witness relating to the war presidency, et cetera. Because the 11A seems to be rather clear on when it may have started and when it may have ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you will have the opportunity to come back to this. Please only be aware that this is a rough 11A as admitted into evidence until now, it is a rough translation. And it would be for the Prosecution now to tender the final and revised translation. That would be then in addition with -1 as usual. That was -2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ms. Karper has on her records an indication that the final translation was submitted to the Defence and Chamber on the 5th of February, it has -- it begins the ERN number 03065755.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The master of our files is Madam Registrar, she has the casting vote. And let's come back to this later. And of course, it's your right to come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I think I was about to show the witness a document -- I believe it was from S115.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, was it among the responsibilities of Mr. Baltic to prepare reports for the Municipal Assembly or for the Crisis Staff regarding technical matters and reports regarding their decisions or conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the technical services of the Municipal Assembly headed by Mr. Baltic had a duty to process documents and data within the purview of the Municipal Assembly, including the takeover by the Crisis Staff of the functions of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at this document, on the report on the implementation of the conclusions of the Prijedor Municipal Crisis Staff, number 1 of the report is "the conclusions for which the public security station is responsible," and there follows 12 different decisions. The first of which is one that came up during the first day of your questioning by Judge Schomburg, the conclusion on banning the release of detainees. Sir, did you ever see this report before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, just as I gave you a precise answer saying that the technical service was serving the Municipal Assembly, I can state with full responsibility that the legislator when adopting this law regarding the Municipal Assembly envisaged that the president of the municipality as a political figure is not required to know the legislation, but he is responsible for the legality of the work of municipal bodies, and he made responsible for this the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, and the law prescribes that only a lawyer by training can occupy this post. As I said, he was required to do this, and I'm saying this now, that the man who drafted this conclusion did not do so in accordance with the law. On the contrary, he drew his own conclusions from the discussion. I, however, stand by my earlier statement that the Crisis Staff was not able to order anything to anyone through a document of this sort, nor could they order the army to take any measures whatsoever. I don't remember having access to this information, to this document that we are discussing now. But this is my explanation as best as I can give it. This man was required, whenever he saw an enactment that was not strictly in accordance with the law, to warn the president that there was a discrepancy, a deviation from the law, and that it shouldn't be done this way. Thank you. I don't know. Maybe I spoke too fast for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, again we're not asking you what the legality is. We're asking you questions about what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I think it would be interesting to hear, was there any such dispute between Mr. Baltic and Dr. Stakic you referred to that should have happened in case a decision, conclusion, would not be in line with the law. Was there ever such a dispute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the secretary was required to tell the president that this enactment should have a basis in law. But whether they had any disputes and whether the secretary indeed drew the president's attention to this, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, would Mr. Drljaca have reported on his implementation of Crisis Staff decisions in your opinion? And for the benefit of counsel, I'm referring to S114 now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the sessions of the Crisis Staff which I attended, there was not a single written document in the form of brief or report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior wherein this body reported or informed the Crisis Staff about the execution of its duties and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what role did you play in your professional capacity in the transfer of the non-Serbian population from Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no role whatsoever in the evacuation of the non-Serbian population from the Serbian -- from the territory of the Prijedor Municipality. All I did was in accordance with the instructions of the government of the Republika Srpska, and that was to issue certificates for the movement of the population outside of the territory of the Prijedor Municipality. And that was in keeping with the current decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Trnopolje camp in order to give people permission to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never visited Trnopolje camp in order to give people permission to leave Prijedor. What happened was this: At the request of -- I think it was the representative of a health-care body, some doctor from Banja Luka, a visit was made to Trnopolje, and it was made by an official of the administration with these documents who issued this document or these documents, these certificates, to the people who happened to be there at the time. I think the name of the doctor is Aleksic. He was a representative of some health-care organisation or maybe the Red Cross or the International Red Cross. I don't remember exactly. I think it was Dr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that the Trnopolje camp was located very close to the railway station in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collection centre in Trnopolje, I have never been there. But I know that it was near the school building which means that it was also close to the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, of large numbers of people, Muslims and Croats, being put on cattle cars and transported out of Prijedor through Banja Luka and out of the area of this Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that, nor was that within the competence of the body that I headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your professional capacity, were you aware of the desperation of Muslim and Croat families to leave Prijedor in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that many people wanted to leave, and many people came to the secretariat where I worked asking for permission to leave the territory of Republika Srpska. All those who submitted the prescribed application in due manner received approvals from the body that I headed. And as for the further organisation of their departure, I don't know anything about it. I think it went through the International Red Cross, but I really don't know for sure. I was not able to follow or monitor all that because I had my own job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for answering part of my question. But the other part was, sir, were you aware of the absolute desperation of these people to leave Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the mindset of any particular person, nor was I able to know that. All I could was to work in accordance with the regulations. All those who applied for documents received them. The situation was chaotic. There were many people, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, I'm not disputing that the Muslims were in the worst in situation. All of them were running away wherever they could. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry sir, we missed the last sentence. If you could repeat it. All we heard was that people were running away wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said after that that of course I'm not putting a mark of equality between all citizens. Of course Muslims and Croats were worse off than Serbs. All people who left -- who could leave left, and all those who applied for permission to my body received permission. And many people left by their own personal vehicles even without any approval, especially those who were on their own, who were fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in that summer of 1992, there were long lines of mainly women standing outside the SUP building waiting to see you or your employees to get permission to leave Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. There were long lines of people waiting for permissions. All of them addressed themselves to the employee who was in charge of the administrative procedure. He was a lawyer by training. They submitted their documents. And as far as we were able, we tried our best to issue those people with documents in accordance with the regulations. I thought that we should do our work in keeping with the law, and that citizens regardless of their ethnicity should be able to exercise their rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, on what floor was your office at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My office was on the first floor, and the work that I talked about right now was being done downstairs on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember that after the broadcast of the first group of foreign journalists to visit the Omarska camp, a great number of foreign journalists descended upon Prijedor, came there, and some of them came to see you? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was not a single journalist who came to visit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two articles, one dated the 15th of August 1992 by Tim Judah. And the second dated the 13th of August, 1992, by Andrej Gustincic. May they -- they are in English only. May they be distributed -- I believe they have been distributed to the parties, but perhaps could be put on the ELMO. Let's start with the one from the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Budimir, this first article appeared on the 15th of August 1992 -- excuse me, that's the date line of the article - in the Times of London. The journalist was Tim Judah. And the article begins by stating: "Slavko Budimir, secretary for the people's defence of the northern Bosnian town of Prijedor, has a fat file of applications before him. They have been filled in by people who want to leave Prijedor. `We have no right to stop anyone who wants to go', he says." The article goes on in the next paragraph to say: "Mr. Budimir says up to 3.000 Muslims have applied to quit Prijedor in the past 15 days, and this has nothing to do with ethnic cleansing." It goes on to quote you as saying, in the same paragraph: "Even some Serbs want to leave. Look, all these forms say they want to go for material reasons. After all, there's not much work here." The journalist says that: "After some pressing, Mr. Budimir eventually admits that some Muslims might want to leave because of insecurity and war psychosis." Do you recall now speaking to two journalists, one of whom spoke Serbian or one of the B/C/S languages, in your office in early August after the initial broadcast from the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. And as far as my memory serves me, for all the duration of the war, I never spoke to a single foreign journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The article goes on to talk about, in the next paragraph, quoting you as saying: "Look, all this has to do with forces over my head. There is no reason for anyone to leave, nor do I support this." First of all, is that true? Would you stand by that statement? Do you think that would be accurate as to how you felt in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said what I think about this. I said that I never spoke to a journalist, and I assert that I never had any contacts with journalists, foreign or otherwise, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could then put the next article, the second page, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order not to create confusion, this last article August 15, 1992 would be provisionally marked S404A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before we leave that article, I'm sorry, there's another quote from Mr. Budimir on the bottom of the first page, the journalists indicate, Mr. Budimir, that they asked you about the detention camps. "Mr. Budimir claimed `nobody is being detained.' When it is pointed out that the whole world has seen the Serb detention camps around Prijedor on television, he says, `they are only for people involved in armed activity and conspiracy.'" Do you have any comment upon this quotation attributed to you in an international newspaper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have any comment because I never spoke to a foreign journalist for all the time the war lasted. I can say that with full responsibility. You can see the entire collection of Kozarski Vjesnik for that period. You can find only one interview, and that had to do with labour duty. You cannot find a single other article or interview with a foreign journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, on the next article --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be marked next in order, the article dated the 13th of August by Mr. Andrej Gustincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provision S405A.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just not to create the confusion, the term "radnovisa" [phoen] is usually in our case translated as "work obligation." Now we heard "labour duty." So maybe now it should be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, on the second page, there's some similar quotations as the last, but I'll read quickly just through a few lines. "On the first floor of the defence ministry building in Prijedor, Slavko Budimir local secretary for defence has a pile of application forms on the desk before him. He insists the Muslims are leaving only because they want to find better jobs elsewhere, looking for medical treatment, or suffering from war psychosis and insecurity." On the last two paragraphs on this page it says: "Visibly uneasy about what he is doing Budimir is quick to disassociate himself from his work. `All this has to do with forces over my head. There's no reason for anyone to leave. Nor do I support this.'" Do you have any comment on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you, sir, that I didn't have any interviews with foreign journalists throughout the war. And I stand by what I am saying firmly with full responsibility. If you want any comments from me nevertheless, then ask me a question that is not related to this, and I will answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many Muslims and Croats did you give permission or permits to leave Prijedor to in the summer, fall -- spring, summer, and fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to this question because I don't have any figures. But I agree with what you say; namely, that many people waited in front of our agency every day waiting for their permissions. I don't know how we can find this figure, but I can say that those people who applied for permission to leave received that permission within a reasonable time. I said that I issued these permissions based on the decree issued by the government, and based on the accompanying documentation that had to be provided together with the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, was this line of people in front of your office something that was well-known to all those who worked in the centre of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who passed by could see lines, queues, before the office, sometimes the queue was longer; sometimes shorter. There were never any huge queues. But depending on the period, the number of people in the line varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that these were the -- the great, great majority were women?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well generally speaking, I can accept your claim that there were more women than men, although there were some men, too. But yes, in principle, there were more women.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, why were there more women in front applying to leave than men?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably because of the general situation in which insecurity prevailed. Men were perhaps afraid to leave their homes, move around. It made no difference to me, woman or man, anybody who came to me and wanted to exercise their legal rights was able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if a woman came to you and told you that her husband, her son, or her brother was in the Omarska camp and she wanted permission to leave for herself and her husband or son, how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parties who came to apply did not contact with me directly. They communicated with the clerk who handled the applications. Only on a couple of occasions every day, if I happened to be there, if the lawyer would come to me and told me that all the documents were in order, I would sign the application, taking the man's word for it, and not doubting that he had followed the entire legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you give instructions as to whether permission should be granted to men who were detained in the Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave no instructions whatsoever. The clerk who handled the applications had his own copy of the decree, and the accompanying enactment which regulated exactly what was supposed to be done. I had no idea who was located where. Instead, if a person filed the application, he was issued with a permission regardless of ethnicity, sex, or any other parameter. People were treated as citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, if someone owned an apartment in Prijedor, did you require them to give up that apartment or to give it to the municipality in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the documents that were required from citizens about to leave the territory, there was a document whereby the citizen had to produce proof that before departing, he returned his apartment to the rightful owner. That means if somebody was a citizen of the Republika Srpska and the apartment was owned by the Celpak company, then the citizen had to produce proof that the apartment he resided in was returned to the Celpak company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What about people who owned a house or apartment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were not required to produce any such document. If somebody owned their own land and apartments or houses, this applied only to people who lived in socially-owned apartments. Private owners were not required to produce this particular document. This documentation is very precisely regulated. We have an exact list of documents required that can be submitted to this Court. That shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown S109.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you, in fact, follow a regulation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina that individuals could only leave with a maximum of 300 deutschmark, or have you heard of this regulation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an instruction which I didn't receive from the Crisis Staff, as you had, of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. This document came to me from my superior body of the ministry, from the secretariat in Banja Luka. And this was being implemented for a short period of time, and I know that there were negotiations in Geneva and that the president of the municipality asked from me to make a photocopy of that enactment to see who was it who issued that order. I gave it to the president of the municipality, and then he sent it either to the president of the municipality or the president's office, and then the president of the state immediately ordered for this enactment to be abolished, and on the following day, this act became null and void. And immediately upon that, we stopped applying that enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say you gave it to the president of the municipality, do you mean Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Dr. Stakic a conduit between the municipality and regional and republic level leaders and bodies? In other words, did he receive instructions from them that were implemented in the municipality, and did he communicate concerns of the municipality to the higher level bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about only this specific case. I was asked to submit a photocopy of this enactment. I gave this to the president, and I believe he told me that he had been required to submit that to the president of the assembly because the president of the state received a complaint in Zurich about charging this fee or something, and that if he was required to abolish that law. As for the levels of communication and the lines of communication between Dr. Stakic and other bodies, I don't know about that. I've already told you that I believe that Dr. Stakic was subordinate to the president of the assembly and the president of the state. Now, who his contacts were with, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told us early in your testimony that there would be occasions, a few occasions, when Dr. Stakic was not present at a meeting because he was out of the municipality. Do you know where he travelled?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't keep a record on Dr. Stakic's movement, nor was I ever responsible for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that when the Executive Board met, Dr. Stakic sometimes attended the meetings of the Executive Board, although not a formal member?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some issues that required the presence of the president of the Municipal Assembly. This was in place even before these events, and this practice still persists. Because the Executive Board is a body that serves the president of the municipality, provides the means for the work of the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly, prepares the general documents and materials that the president of the Municipal Assembly is supposed to communicate to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions at this time. We have not yet admitted 405. We would move to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have a number of documents not yet admitted. We'll come back to this later. In terms of superiority and subordination, could one say that the Executive Board was subordinate to the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the Executive Board was subordinated to the Municipal Assembly. And the president of the Municipal Assembly chairs over the sessions of the Municipal Assembly, and the Executive Board reported on its work and was responsible to the Municipal Assembly, which was presided by the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I open the discussion on the two documents, S404A and S405A, I regard it as my obligation to recall that what I told you at the beginning of your testimony. And this is the risk that you're running when testifying in a way foreseen under Rule 91. This would be a false testimony under solemn declaration punishable with a fine of 100.000 Euro or a term of imprisonment of seven years or both. You have seen the two documents, one appearing in The Times, and one from Reuters. Reuters is a news agency. So, in fact, it might be -- it might be but we can come back to this later by hearing Mr. Tim Judah in person, it might be that the primary source for this is the Reuters agency report of August 13th. Therefore, my question: Have you ever seen or were you ever visited by Mr. Andrej Gustincic? Maybe he didn't appear with you as a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. journalist. Because I think you as an intelligent person, you know how easy it can be to -- just to call both witnesses, maybe they still have a tape or own notes, and then you will run into a difficult situation. And it's for a judge also to prevent crimes to be committed. And therefore, in your own interest, I have to ask you once more, did you ever discuss these issues in Document 405A with a Mr. Andrej Gustincic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate you drawing my attention to this, and I do feel the responsibility with this regard. As far as I can remember, if my memory serves me well, I really don't remember that a journalist visited me ever or asked me any questions. I don't have any reason whatsoever to withhold the truth if I can remember things. I would answer all the questions that are in this article. But at this moment, I can't remember that. This person may have come and stepped into my office for five minutes, maybe accompanied by somebody else. Maybe he didn't introduce himself. Maybe they did talk to me, but I never realised that that was an interview. Anybody could enter my office and ask me questions. I never asked for any protection either by the police or the army. Maybe people stepped into my office, asked me questions that later on appeared in an article. But I can't remember that. I simply -- I talked to everybody, to a number of people.
