But I claim with full responsibility that I never received somebody who would have introduced himself as a journalist. I never spoke to a journalist in that capacity. Maybe it was somebody else who came to my office and whatever they asked me, I answered. I've spoke the truth all the time. And all I want to say is the truth. So whatever questions you want to ask me, the Prosecution, the Defence, and you, Your Honours, I will answer your questions. You know that times were really difficult, and I abide by my testimony that I really do not -- I'm not aware that I had contacts with any journalists. And if you believe and if you deem it important to come to the truth, I will answer to all the questions that may be put to me by the Prosecutor. So if the Prosecutor wants to ask me the same questions again, I will answer them. Thank you, Your Honour, for warning me and for drawing my attention to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So indeed, I want you to give you a second chance and draw the attention of the representative of the Prosecution that, in fact, in the article by Tim Judah, reference is made to Andrej Gustincic of Reuters news agency. But based on the content, I would like you to ask the same line of questions once again related to the content, whether based on the content the witness is able to recall what he allegedly stated. You started with 404.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm now going to 405 and looking for where it begins to speak about visiting Mr. Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The article, Mr. Budimir, by Mr. Gustincic, and there has been some testimony in this trial that he speaks B/C/S, states: "On the first floor of the defence ministry building in Prijedor, Slavko Budimir, local secretary for defence, has a pile of application forms on the desk before him. He insists that the Muslims are leaving only because they want to find better jobs elsewhere, go for medical treatment, or are suffering from `war psychosis and insecurity'. Some Serbs also want to leave, he says. But closer inspection of the forms show that out of some 3.000 people, only about 400 are Serbs, and most of them are from mixed families. Visibly uneasy about what he is doing, Budimir is quick to dissociate himself from his work. `All this has to do with forces over my head. There is no reason for anyone to leave, nor do I support this.'" The remainder of the article deals with the journalists speaking to some of the women, or at least one young woman who had been in the line outside. Do you have any recollection, sir, of any foreigner -- or perhaps he didn't appear to be a foreigner, a person speaking your language, speaking to you prior to the 13th of August, probably between the 6th of August and the 13th of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to offer my comment: In this article, it says that there was a pile of papers in front of me. These papers were never in front of me. They were always in front of my official, the lawyer that was dealing with these papers. And in the second part, it says "when by closer inspection you can see that there are so many of these and so many of those," really, nobody would have allowed this person a closer inspection of these documents. So whatever it says here is simply not true. And the third question, I don't know what you want me to say. I will answer your third question. Can you just repeat what the third part of your question was. About the reasons why these people were moving or something like that, in relation to what it says here. Maybe you could repeat that part of the question. I want to make myself clear on that part of the question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll just quote what the article says you said about people leaving. The article quotes you as: "Insisting that the Muslims are leaving only because they want to find better jobs elsewhere, go for medical treatment, or are suffering from `war psychosis and insecurity.'" It says that you told him: "Some Serbs also want to leave."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that everybody was leaving, and those who applied to the Ministry of Defence as citizens and asked for permission to leave, we would enable them to do so through prescribed procedures. As for the reasons for which they were leaving, I've already said that everybody was leaving and that I didn't make any distinction between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. But I also said that Croats and Muslims were worse off than the Serbs. But everybody was leaving. And as for other reasons given here, they can apply but I must say that the -- what I think is the most important reason for which they were leaving, it is not in the Serbian, so I don't know. But it seems to me that it is -- this is what I said. I don't know -- I don't remember what was the reason given, if somebody can translate those reasons to me because they are only in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe it's not necessary to repeat once again that this certain paragraph quoting you as "he insists that the Muslims are leaving because they want to find better jobs elsewhere, go for medical treatment or are suffering from `war psychosis and insecurity.'" This would be totally in line with your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed, I certainly didn't say that they were leaving first and foremost because they wanted to find a better job. The primary reason would be objective circumstances, and then other reasons would follow. So I'm sure I didn't say that the most important reason for their departure was their wish to find better jobs. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And these most important reasons would be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most important reasons was the situation in town, disrespect for law and order, plunder, killings, murders, and this had effect on everybody making it the primary reason for departure of everybody. And then other reasons mentioned here and others would follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, do you want to be confronted with the other article as well a second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will leave it up to you. But you have already said yourself that this article may have originated from another source, so that this is not an original article, but that there is another primary source of that article. But if you think I should be confronted with it again, I will certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I stated that it might be a secondary source only, but as to the fact there were some additional quotations quoted as your own words, I would believe it would be only fair to you -- for you to be confronted with these quotations once again in Document S404.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the article by Tim Judah, S404, the article begins: "Slavko Budimir, secretary for the people's defence of the northern Bosnian town of Prijedor, has a fat file of applications before him. They have been filled in by people who want to leave Prijedor. `We have no right to stop anyone who wants to go.'" First, sir, do you think you would have said that to someone if they had asked you, that you had no right to stop anyone who wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to say firstly that it really doesn't make sense to quote from a different article within this context. It cannot be a quotation if it was transferred from another article. And as for the question that you have put to me, I neither prevented or stopped people from doing anything. I just implemented the regulations in the way that they were worded, and I worked with all the citizens in my capacity as the head of the body that I headed. So this would be my answer to you and to this Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. To continue with how this article quotes you, it says: "Mr. Budimir says up to 3.000 Muslims have applied to quit Prijedor in the past 15 days, and this has nothing to do with ethnic cleansing. `Even some Serbs want to leave,' Mr. Budimir says. `Look, all these forms say they want to go for material reasons. After all, there's not much work here.'" And then the journalist writes: "After some pressing Mr. Budimir eventually admits that some Muslims might want to leave because of `insecurity and war psychosis.'" In the next paragraph, it quotes you as saying: "Look, all this has to do with forces over my head. There is no reason for anyone to leave, nor do I support this." The next paragraph, it quotes you as saying: "Nobody is being detained." When asked about the pictures of people in Omarska and Trnopolje camps, you said: "They were only for people involved in armed activity or conspiracy."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO BUDIMIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are fabrications. I never uttered these words. I believe that I was very precise talking about all of these issues. And if there are other concrete questions, I'm willing to answer them. As for this, I claim that these are fabrications. I've never said that, and you could have concluded that from my previous testimony. I've already told you what my views are on all of this, and I don't see the need to go over the same grounds again. I apologise, if I may add something else: Once again, I would like to thank the Presiding Judge to give me the opportunity to overcome this problem in this way, and I hope that this may help to avoid any problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clear statement, Mr. Budimir. And I have now to ask the Defence, objections against the admission into evidence of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. We do object for these documents to be admitted. And I don't know if the Prosecution has further data regarding these statements made by those journalists. And we would like to cross those journalists if Your Honours think they should be called. But before there is testimony, I think that they should be admonished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not at the moment have any further information. I asked to have the documents admitted. As Your Honours know, hearsay is admissible. The Court may consider the fact that they are hearsay and the witnesses are not here. I would also refer the Court to the decision, fairly recent of the Appeals Chamber, on the subpoena for Jonathan Randall, and the criteria that the Appeals Chamber asked the Trial Chambers to look at, basically indicating a preference that in cases where the evidence is not - and I'm going to misstate the standard because I don't have it on the tip of my tongue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's quite clear that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -- the high standard that journalists should not be called. These are definitely war correspondents who were in Prijedor in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But for the second part of the question put by Mr. Lukic, does the Prosecution have the original articles, the two of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't believe so, but we can check. This is obviously -- it appears to me to be something taken off the internet or off some type of news service, indicating that these were 645 stories and various numbers that were printed off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it could be helpful to have the articles as such in its entirety because sometimes we have the -- we have to make the unfortunate experience that what was -- what is seen on the internet is not the entire article or only part or sometimes even misleading. I don't want to say that this is true for these concrete articles, but we have to take care. And therefore I would ask the Prosecution, if possible, to produce these two articles in its -- in a copy of the original. Applying the standards in this Trial Chamber on the admission of evidence, only as to the mere fact that these documents were discussed in Court and the witness made reference and clarification on these documents, it is absolutely necessary to admit these documents in evidence. Therefore, the article from 15th of August 1992 is admitted under S404A. And the other one from the 13th of August 1992 as S405A. Then we have the problem with Document S11. And I was just informed that the final transcript of the whole tape S11 was until now only distributed to the Defence and the Judges, but never admitted into evidence. Therefore, my question, first, to the Prosecution, does the Prosecution tender the entire transcript of S11?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections by the Defence. This is opposed to the rough translation in part, the entire final and revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're still examining that, Your Honour, but we do have an objection based on the final translation because we think it quite frankly doesn't match the tape that's presented. But having just reviewed it this afternoon, we would like to reserve it and we think S11 comes closer, at least in our opinion, to what the actual tape and conversations or interviews were with the participants. I think the Court can compare the two and make that decision on its own, but we would like the right to examine it with the tape contemporaneously and then look at the entirety of the document as well as the tape. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The entire transcript of the tape S11 admitted into evidence as Exhibit S11A/B-2. Anything else for today? And may I ask, what is the time estimate for additional questions to put to the witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we can finish in less than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we would then proceed in the following order: That we first would hear Witness 006, and then at least try to hear the second Defence witness by tomorrow. If there are any problems, please let us know. But if we could finish with two additional witnesses, it would facilitate the work of the victim and witness unit and, of course, of the witnesses having the right to come back to their home country immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to advise the Court with respect to Witness 006, obviously he'll be prepared and is prepared to proceed tomorrow. The second witness just arrived this afternoon. So we don't and have not met with him. We just said hello. We're meeting with him this evening, so we did not anticipate, since he just arrived today, that he would be going on tomorrow. And we are caught in a little difficult situation because obviously the proffers are not complete and they won't be complete until very late this evening once we've had an opportunity to meet with him. He did just arrive late this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We leave it in this case to the parties. Your preference would be to proceed immediately after Witness 006 immediately with Mr. Travar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The opinion of the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Either is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we have to decide on this and let you know as soon as possible and as soon as practical. This concludes today's hearing. We are sitting tomorrow in Courtroom II once again, in the afternoon, a quarter past 2.00. And therefore, the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 15 minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
